reconcile.connective: JFB argues Jesus was not excluding himself from goodness — that would contradict Scripture — but redirecting the man toward recognizing his true nature.

discrepancy.connective: Skeptic Paul Carlson calls this reply 'an embarrassment to the church,' reading it as evidence Jesus did not consider himself sinless.

skeptic.name: Paul Carlson
skeptic.attribution: Paul Carlson, "New Testament Contradictions" (Internet Infidels Modern Library, 1995)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Did our Lord mean then to teach that God only ought to be called "good?" Impossible, for that had been to contradict all Scripture teaching, and His own, too (Psa 112:5; Mat 25:21; Tit 1:8). Unless therefore we are to ascribe captiousness to our Lord, He could have had but one object--to raise the youth's ideas of Himself, as not to be classed merely with other "good masters," and declining to receive this title apart from the "One" who is essentially and only "good."
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers whether Jesus denied his own goodness in the Synoptic exchange, arguing the deflection is rhetorical redirection toward his divine identity rather than a self-exclusion from goodness — the exact tension with John's self-applied 'good shepherd.'

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats Mark 10:18 directly under 'Sinfulness' (Doctrinal Discrepancies, p. 160), explaining 'none good but God' as a claim about absolute, underived goodness, with human goodness only relative and derivative — not a self-denial of goodness.
